360: I have sailed to the far corners of the world. I remember them as wet, and quite far away.
361: People ask about the exotic places I've seen. I mostly saw the same six seabirds, hoping for scraps.
362: I've crossed more seas than I can count. On each, something slid off the table, and I let it go.
363: I've been everywhere by boat. The ocean, I have learned, has no signs telling you which part you are in.
364: The sea has taken me to distant shores. I mostly recall the sea, and a strong wish for dry socks.
365: I've sailed for decades. My memories are a blur of horizon, salt, and one very good soup.
366: People think a sailor's life is romantic. It is mostly rope, weather, and looking at more water.
367: I have seen sights no landlocked soul has seen. I described them once as blue, then more blue.
368: I could navigate by the stars. Lately I navigate by whoever seems most confident on deck.
369: Every port looks different and every sea looks the same. I have accepted the sea's routine.
370: I've sailed the whole globe. People ask about the sunsets. After enough of them, I mostly just check if it is bedtime.
371: The waves rock me to sleep every night. On land, the floor refuses to do its part.
372: I've weathered great storms. I remember them the way one remembers a bad meeting: loudly, and wetly.
373: Ask me the best place I've sailed to and I will think, then describe the harbor with the emptiest dock.
374: I know a hundred knots and I use the same three. The other ninety-seven are for showing off.
375: The horizon is my whole view. It never gets closer. We have an understanding, the horizon and I.
376: I've spent so long at sea that a puddle now feels like coming home.
377: People want tales of high adventure. My best one is about a very large wave I mostly slept through.
378: I've dropped anchor in more harbors than I can name, which is handy, as I can name none.
379: The sea is my whole career and I still could not tell you what is at the bottom of it.
380: I run the harbor. I do not leave the harbor. I still, somehow, manage to get seasick.
381: Every boat here answers to me. The seagulls answer to no one, and they are quite smug about it.
382: I've stood at this dock for years. I can recite the tide's schedule, but never remember my own lunch.
383: I direct ships in and out all day. The one place I never go is out.
384: The sailors sail off to adventure. I stay behind and fill out a small form for every one that leaves.
385: I know every vessel in this harbor by name. I have set foot on precisely none of them.
386: People assume a harbor master loves the sea. I love it deeply, from a firm and unmoving distance.
387: I keep order among a hundred boats. Order among a hundred boats is a generous word for it.
388: My whole world is this one patch of water and its comings and goings. The comings, mostly.
389: I watch the tides all day. They come, they go, they never once ask my opinion.
390: I have the finest view of the water, and I spend most of the day looking down at a clipboard instead.
391: Ships arrive with grand stories. I nod, wave them to a berth, and return to my very still chair.
392: I signal the boats where to go. Where I go is the same office, every day, at the same slow pace.
393: The harbor never sleeps, which is a kind way of saying neither, most nights, do I.
394: I am in charge of everything that floats here. I, personally, would rather not float at all.
395: Every captain thinks their arrival is special. To me it is one more day, with a bit more rope involved.
396: People ask me the fastest way to the sea. I point straight ahead. It is always, reliably, straight ahead.
397: My desk faces the water. The water faces me back. Between us we have solved nothing.
398: I count the boats in, I count the boats out. The numbers should match. It's a good day when they do.
399: I stay firmly on land while everyone drifts off. Someone has to be here when they all drift back in.
